_doc: Single source for SD-95's technology choices; see SD-08/stack.json for the format. `how` is spoken, so it carries no code; keep summary cells under 36 characters.

stack.heading: Servicing DB: PostgreSQL for ledger and queue
stack.title: The ledger and the work queue in one transaction
stack.pick: PostgreSQL 16, partitioned by month, one writer to the ledger
stack.why: A collection is a state change, a pair of balanced ledger entries and an event. They must commit together, and one writer to the ledger keeps the order simple.
stack.how: Ledger entries are double entry: each transaction's lines sum to zero, checked by a deferred constraint at commit. Payment intents are rows with a state, changed by conditional updates. The due-item queue is a table selected with row locks that skip rows already taken. The outbox row commits with the entry. Tables are partitioned by month, so old months become read-only and cheap.
stack.detail: A single logical writer to the ledger removes cross-writer ordering problems; throughput is a few thousand entries a second.
rejected: A message broker as the queue
A second system to keep consistent with the ledger. The table queue commits with the entry.
Multiple ledger writers
Ordering, locking and deadlock handling for no throughput we need.
A key-value store
No multi-row transaction, so balance and intent could disagree.
summary: State, entries and queue commit together
stack.course: theory/03 (partitioning and storage) and theory/07 (correctness under failure)
drill: A worker takes a due item and crashes before finishing. What happens to it?

The row lock is released with the transaction; the item is still due and another worker takes it. The idempotent intent key makes a second attempt harmless. The trap is marking taken before doing the work.
a lock released on crash; an idempotent intent key

stack.heading: Dispatcher: a token bucket per rail
stack.title: A worker that spends each rail's limit on purpose
stack.pick: Go worker, a token bucket per rail, a plan of the day
stack.why: A bank-debit rail and a card processor have limits, cut-offs and a cost. Firing everything at midnight on the first would break them.
stack.how: The dispatcher takes due intents and spends tokens from the rail's bucket. The day is planned backwards from each rail's cut-off, with the largest and riskiest items first and a jittered spread. Each call carries our reference. If a rail is down the bucket stops, and intents wait instead of retrying in a storm.
stack.detail: A card retry and a bank-debit fallback are separate intents with their own keys.
rejected: Firing every due item at once
The first of the month would breach the bank limit and the processor's rate.
Retrying every failure immediately
A retry storm on a rail that is already struggling.
summary: The day is planned, not fired
drill: It is the first of the month and the card processor is down. What does the dispatcher do?
Stop spending that rail's tokens, keep intents waiting, protect the customer from late fees, and resume slowly when it returns. The trap is retrying in a storm.
pause the rail; protect the customer; resume slowly

stack.heading: Resolver: unknown to final
stack.title: A worker that turns unknown into a final answer
stack.pick: Scheduled worker, inquiry by reference, backoff, an alert at a deadline
stack.why: A call that timed out may have moved money. Unknown is a state with an owner, and only an inquiry can end it.
stack.how: The resolver selects unknown intents past a minimum age and asks the rail by our reference. It applies the answer with a conditional update from unknown. Backoff stretches from seconds to hours, and an intent that stays unknown for a day pages a person. The age of the unknown queue is a metric.
stack.detail: A late webhook and the resolver cannot both apply; the conditional update decides.
rejected: Retrying the original call
If it landed, the customer is charged twice.
Marking a timeout as failed
A debit that succeeded is shown as failed, and the loan is wrong.
summary: Unknown has an owner and an age
drill: A debit times out. What is the state and what moves money next?
Unknown. The resolver asks the rail by reference until it answers, and only that answer moves money. The trap is a retry or a failed mark.
unknown; inquiry by reference; the answer moves money

stack.heading: File ingest: raw first, then parse
stack.title: Settlement and return files stored raw before they are parsed
stack.pick: Object storage for raw files, a batch parser, counts and totals checked first
stack.why: Returns arrive weeks later, in files. A parse bug must never lose the original.
stack.how: Each file is stored raw in object storage with a hash, then parsed by a batch job. Counts and totals are checked against the file's trailer before any line is applied. Each line is matched to an intent by reference, and applying a return is an idempotent ledger transaction. A file that fails a check is quarantined, not half applied.
stack.detail: The raw copy lets a fixed parser replay old files.
rejected: Parsing on arrival
A bug loses the original, and a half-applied file is hard to unwind.
Streaming each line as it comes
Files are daily; a stream adds state for no freshness gain.

stack.heading: Reconciliation: three-way
stack.title: Ledger, rail and bank matched every day, line by line
stack.pick: Batch pipeline over the ledger, the rail's file and the bank's statement, by reference
stack.why: The ledger, the rail and the bank are three versions of the truth. Differences are breaks, and each break has an owner.
stack.how: A daily job matches every ledger entry to the rail's settlement line and to the bank statement by reference. Two-way agreement is a match; a line missing on one side, a different amount or a duplicate is a break. Breaks carry an age and an owner, and each resolution is a new ledger entry. A total that differs from the bank's by four hundred dollars is explained line by line, not plugged.
stack.detail: Counts and sums are compared first, so a truncated file stops the job.
rejected: Matching on amount and date alone
Equal payments on the same day are ambiguous.
A monthly reconciliation
Breaks age for weeks and the month-end close becomes an investigation.
drill: Our ledger says four hundred dollars more than the bank. How do you find it?
Match line by line by reference across ledger, rail and bank; the break is a line missing or doubled on one side. Fix it with a new entry. The trap is a plug figure.
match by reference; fix with a new entry

stack.heading: Policy: terms, waterfall and fees as data
stack.title: Policy as versioned data, owned by risk and legal
stack.pick: A rules service, versioned terms, a payment waterfall, a fee table
stack.why: Terms, the order in which a payment is applied and fees change with law and product. They must change without a deploy and be reproducible later.
stack.how: The policy service holds versioned terms: the schedule rules, the waterfall of interest, fees and principal, and the fee table. Every ledger entry records the policy version used. A refund in the middle of a loan is a transaction plus a new schedule version computed from the policy at that date.
stack.detail: Risk and legal approve a version; engineering does not edit it.
rejected: Terms in code
A deploy per change, and no way to reproduce what applied on a past date.
Terms in each service
Two services would apply different rules to one payment.

stack.heading: Servicing API: idempotent and quote-aware
stack.title: An API that quotes a payoff and applies refunds safely
stack.pick: Go service, an idempotency key on every write, payoff quotes that list what is in flight
stack.why: Customers and agents retry. A payoff quote that ignores a debit in flight is wrong the moment it is paid.
stack.how: Every write carries an idempotency key under a unique constraint. A payoff quote lists the principal, accrued interest and every intent in flight, with the quote's expiry. A payoff with a debit in flight either waits for the debit to resolve or nets it, and says which. A refund is a ledger transaction with a new schedule version, never an edit.
stack.detail: Refunds are limited by a conditional update on the refunded total.
rejected: Quoting from the ledger balance only
An in-flight debit changes the answer after the customer pays.
Editing the schedule in place
History must be append-only, or a dispute cannot be reproduced.

1: Treating a timeout as a failure
the debit may have landed; unknown is a state and an inquiry ends it.
2: Firing every due item at midnight on the first
the bank-debit limit and the rail rate break; plan the day backwards from the cut-off.
3: returns arrive weeks later; RETURNED is a state and a reversal is a transaction.
4: Editing the schedule in place for a refund
history must be append-only; a refund is a transaction and a new schedule version.
5: Quoting the payoff from the ledger balance alone
an in-flight debit changes it; the quote lists what is in flight.
6: Plugging the difference to the bank
the break is a line missing or doubled; match every line three ways by reference.
7: Retrying a down rail until it returns
a retry storm; pause, resolve, protect the customer, resume slowly.
8: breaks age for weeks; watch the money funnel and the files daily.
